[ALUSI-FULL:v27p129#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Addressing the Hour as if someone could ask it why it came is a representational metaphor, either imagined or taken literally.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p129#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | كاذبة may derive from كذبت نفسه or كذبته, when one’s self deceives, indulges distant hopes, and emboldens a person to attempt a great undertaking.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p129#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الكشف | reports | Al-Kashf says the lām in that interpretation also marks time: no self will encourage its owner to think it can endure the Event’s severity.
[ELMALILI:56:1-24/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | He prefers the apparent construction in which verse 2 supplies the answer to the conditional in verse 1.
[ELMALILI:56:1-24/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | One rendering says no person will call the Resurrection’s occurrence false.

[ELMALILI:56:1-24/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Wuqūʿ means falling; waqʿa is the noun for one forceful fall, later used for a great blow or crisis and sometimes specifically for war.
[ELMALILI:56:1-24/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | People may deny Resurrection before it comes, but once it occurs no one can deny it; all must affirm it and cannot escape its impact and upheaval.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p281/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Al-kadhiba may be an active participle of intransitive kadhiba, with a suppressed feminine nafs: no soul will deny or lie about the Resurrection once it occurs.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p281/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | On that reading, deniers claim the Resurrection will not occur, but when it happens every soul will believe it and none will still deny it or lie about it.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p281/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse warns deniers that the Resurrection will prove their error, leaving them disgraced and foolish in the assembly of the gathered.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p282/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling a failed cause a lie extends the word metaphorically: Abu Ali al-Farisi says lying is a kind of speech, and Arabic can attribute speech or lying to something that does not speak.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p282/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abu Ali also cites the phrase about garments lying as an example of using falsehood beyond literal speech.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p282/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lām in liwaq'atiha marks time, like the lām in commands to pray at the sun's decline and to divorce for the waiting period; this grew from lām of specification. | mentions 17:78, 65:1, 7:143
